Yeah.

First and foremost was people.
Are there smart, driven, good people to work with, you know, that I had an alignment of

Who I was going to be working for for sure is a big piece of that.
I'm at a point in my career where I feel like I can be picky about the products I go and

And then the third thing was the problems.
What are the problems I can go in and solve?
Am I going to add a lot of value to the place I'm going and are those interesting problems

Got to know a lot of the people that I was going to be working with.
Shopify is known for great people and it's known for its values and culture.
Shopify speaks for itself and the thought of doing a big scratch build, taking a sales

It was a pretty easy decision from there.
And for those on the call, it sounded like you had an interesting pivot point that took

So you mentioned being in the boiler room.
What was that transition like?
So I spent five years at a company selling conferences and events, like not a great company,

And it was a great place to grow up as a salesperson and it wasn't easy and you really just had

So that was a great five years.
I loved my time.
I was really young.
So the fact that this was a bit of a crazy company didn't affect me.
It was all fun.
I was just having a blast being in sales and sales leadership.
And at one point, then I said, okay, I really want to get into the technology space.
That's where things had been going and knew that my resume didn't really translate.
And just because the company was sort of unknown, people in technology are pretty snooty about

I was really thoughtful about how I was going to make that happen.

So I just started cold calling people, like heads of sales at companies that I respected

I just wanted his advice.
I was just trying to reach out to people to get some advice and insight, knowing that

And then through that conversation, he was talking about problems in the business or

I was like, oh, well, what about X, Y, and Z?
One thing led to another and he basically said, hey, do you want to come do this for

And that was it.
I just needed a chance because I think then, you know, we're snooty about people who don't

But then as soon as you have the technology brand on your resume, oh, you're like a technology

So it was much easier to go from the next thing to the next thing.
It's kind of like that old adage, if you ask for money, you'll get advice.
Ask for advice, you'll get money twice.
Yeah.
So, I mean, a really interesting stat here.
As of May, Shopify surpassed the RBC to take title of Canada's most valuable company.
Clearly that was all you and your team's work.
Of course.
It's no secret that due to the worldwide pandemic, the mandated shutdown of most retail stores
this year opened up a massive opportunity for Shopify to grow in the brick and mortar
market.
So anticipating an immediate surge in new retail customers, what did you do quickly
but effectively to set your team up for success?
So there's a lot in this question and even sort of that baseline assumption that we knew
this was going to create a surge in the retail sector wasn't really known at the time.
Like no one knew what was going to happen.
There was still in those early days, the possibility that this just like crushed everything and
was bad for Shopify.
It seems crazy to say that now, but at the time, so much different information, there's
so little known about the situation and you're just scrambling to figure things out.
So nothing was really assumed or known.
But you could quickly tell within a couple of weeks that a lot of people were going to
be hurting, especially brick and mortar retailers.
And so this is a top-down thing all the way from our CEO, Toby.
He basically said, rip up every plan, start from scratch.
Like I don't care what you were working on before, whether it's a product roadmap or
an investment plan or what we were trying to build into the commercial organization.
Like start from scratch again and start from the merchant.
So knowing what is happening in the market, what do we need to do to help merchants survive
and thrive?
And so certainly for our group, that mandate was, how do we take brick and mortar retailers
with very little online presence and help them get online really fast so they can survive?
So there was a huge product investment in helping this transition.
We'll talk a little bit later about the initiative with Government of Canada.
Basically everybody was given the mandate in every part of the company that we're here
to go fight for our merchants.
And that's the only thing that mattered.
And so for us, we basically just looked at every plan and asked ourselves, what is more
of a long-term bet and not an immediate payoff for our merchants today?
Let's defer a bunch of those.
And we just started to go to work and so much was changing.
It's funny that it's hard to put yourself back there and think about how ambiguous things
were.
But things were changing every week, the economy coming to a crash and everybody dying was
a possibility one day and then the next day it was like, oh, it's only the flu.
Those were real oscillations that everybody was having.
So we just tried to stay close to the ground floor.
We were updating our messaging.
We were really leaning into the reps in terms of coaching.
Just lead with empathy.
Just hear what's going on and really just try to seek to help these people and help
them make a good decision to move their business forward.
So a big piece of that was just listening and reacting on the fly.
And then more tactically, we played a bunch with our messaging.
We changed the tone of our emails and our cadences and how we approached calls and the
questions we opened up with and how we went for closes.
All of that had to evolve given the environment.
And then just coaching, coaching, coaching.
We really tried to lean into the front line leads, helping them help people.
Because the other huge part of this whole thing was we had to take care of our team.
We can't help merchants if our team is in a really tough spot.
So stressful and it was so overwhelming.
So also leaning into empathy as a leader, that was really critical for us.
And just helping our front line managers navigate a completely unprecedented situation where
there was no playbook.
It's so interesting that arguably the largest tech company now, largest company in Canada

pivot.
But as you mentioned, every single day there were things that were just being presented
that were just completely on the other side of the spectrum.
So what advice would you give business owners who have to make these quick decisions when
changes in the market are this abrupt?
You mentioned a lot of things about empowering your team and leading with empathy and scratching
the previous playbooks and plans that you had in place and really starting from the
ground up.
Is there anything else that you could maybe harp on for the business owners that are online
right now?
Yeah.
And do you mean business owners as in like retailers of business owners as in people
running technology companies?
Yeah, let's do both.
Okay.
So I'll give the non-technology answer.
I'm asking the questions here, okay?
That's good.
First is try not to panic, I think is important.
So as much as you can, take a deep breath and try to manage your emotions so that you're
making the wisest decisions possible.
And the way the brain works is when you're in that sort of amygdala fight or flight response
your rational thinking, your prefrontal cortex shuts down.
Your body is wired to sort of turn off that part of your brain which thinks slower, which
is that frontal cortex which actually helps you think through things rationally.
So there's a physiological thing that's happening here where if you're in this amygdala response
mode or amygdala hijack, you're not going to make great decisions.
So first, try to calm yourself, try to calm your team and make reasonable rational decisions.
I think that seems fluffy but is really critical.
Check in with your team and try to help people navigate these things personally.
And then when it comes to making business decisions, collect the best data that you
have.
We sprinted pretty fast to try to set up dashboards, new ways of monitoring the business so that
we were on a daily basis seeing the trends and the fluctuations in our operation.
So collect the data that you've got, try to use that to the best of your ability.
I spoke with a lot of people in my network, so reaching out to other people for other
perspectives and every company is different, so you're not going to rely on one opinion
or you're not going to overly rely on outside voices.
But just having a network of people that you can go to and check in because there's always
somebody that's dealing with what you're dealing with or has dealt with it in the past.
And I believe community is really important, especially in these situations.
And then read.
I was reading a lot.
I had big chunks of my day that were just trying to keep on top of the latest happenings
and the latest thinking because there was a lot of blogging, there was a lot of medium
articles, there was a lot of stuff in the revenue leadership group that I'm involved
in.
So just trying to take in as much information as possible was really helpful for us.
So it's like data, different perspectives, and just like slowing down, I think, slowing
down and trying to think as rationally as possible would be like crisis management tips
I would give.
And on that note, so you mentioned a book in the rapid fire.
Could you maybe just tell us a little bit about that book?
And was that something that you opened up around this time?
It wasn't.

And this was one of the earlier books written on how to build good sales infrastructure

So a lot of that content is now in a lot of different places people have borrowed and

You'll read blogs and blogs and blogs that are just sort of like a paraphrasing of that

So it's a great one to get a foundational understanding of how sales works and especially
if you're an engineer, like how to think about this in a way that is familiar.
I didn't necessarily open it.
Those are things that it wasn't as relevant for this situation, like a lot of the perspective
I was leaning into was some of our Shopify leadership, just because the level of craft
and the level of business acumen is so interesting or is so great.
And the problem solving approach is different than I think what you see in a lot of places.
It wasn't like, oh, batten down the hatches, think about your financial runway.
I mean, we're not a startup, so that's not as big of a conversation, but it wasn't like
a financially driven conversation.
Think about all the ways that you can cut costs and prepare for this thing.
The emergency response was like, how do we help our merchants?
And so that is unique.
And so I was really trying to lean into that.
Gotcha.
And so Shopify recently partnered with the government of Alberta, or Alberta, wow, that's

to bring more small businesses and just help them adapt to the new economy, the digital

So it seems like Shopify is becoming much more than an e-commerce platform here.
And having to say in terms of how Canadian residents find that next thing or find that
next level of growth.
Can you speak more about this initiative and how it's helped entrepreneurs across the country

So this is a good example of rip up every plan and go find a way to help merchants.
This thing got spun up in record time as a way to help Canadian businesses adapt.
And so the components, there's an extended free trial of all the tools.
There's a custom learning pathway that the team put together to help people take their

We provided a bunch of enhanced support.
There's free hardware that we threw into it.
So a whole bunch of great stuff was put into this initiative and the partnership team and

So it's been really successful so far.
I think a lot of businesses are using this as an opportunity to digitize.
And this will have a lasting effect.
I think this is a permanent shift that we're going to see in the market.
So it was a really cool example of everything stops but helping our merchants.
And this program was something that would have taken months and months, if not years,
to do and we got done in record time.
And then there was a bunch of other stuff that the company did to help these type of
merchants.
So we reprioritized the product roadmap.
We launched curbside pickup and local delivery in record time.
There was massive changes made internally in terms of the product vision, which is a

And big changes were made, which was super cool to see.
It was fun to be a part of.
Especially for how big you guys are and with everything going on, to make drastic changes

So was that something that was then adopted globally outside of Canada?
So it's a Canadian program right now, and lots more being done on similar stuff.
Gotcha.
So, I mean, a sales strategy is very rarely a one-size-fits-all solution.
And what works for one company's product might not necessarily work for another's.
But, I mean, as a seasonal sales expert from selling for conferences and in the boiler
room to now focusing on working with Shopify, you must have some tried-and-true tips for
what sticks and what doesn't when it comes to selling technology.
For our tech startups that are in attendance here today, what advice would you give them,
give relatively new companies who are in the process of implementing a sales strategy or
who have started to implement a sales strategy, but maybe it could be breaking or they may
not be getting the results that they're looking for?
And where can they maybe start?
Yeah.
So in the early days, a few things that I think are really important to keep in mind
is one, stay laser-focused on your customer and tied at the hip with them.
So you can't be all things to all people, especially in the early days, super constrained
on resources.
You can only do so many things, whether it's building products or investing in go-to-market.
So I think having a pretty specific understanding of the value you provide and who's going to
see that value is important and staying really closely tied to those customers.
So I think there's a lot of times an over-investment in sales early compared to service and customer
success because the greatest snowball effect you can have in your business is a bunch of
super satisfied customers that are willing to sing your praises and that's the best marketing
you could possibly have.
Whether it's getting on reference calls or speaking about you in the market, providing
real value to customers and treating them really well, I think is the quickest way to
go from a really small handful of customers to a meaningful amount.
The other thing I would say in the early days is really critical is knowing where to spend
your time, like what type of individuals to spend those resources on.
And so as much as we, especially in the early days, craft like these fairly artistically
drawn ROI statements and like, this is all the value, this is the return, and how fast
you're going to get the payback, that's all great, but buyers aren't going to believe
it from a startup.
And the earlier we can understand that, the better.
And so the types of people you want to spend time on are not the individuals that are really
going to evaluate you on a spreadsheet and make sure the ROI numbers all line up.
That's a pretty conservative approach to buying products.
And a conservative approach is not going to lead you to doing business with a startup.
You need to find change agents.
You need to find people who are contrarians in their industry that are going to hear your
message and be like, yeah, this market is screwed up.
We do need this type of thing.
And they have to want to do business with you for more reasons than like a very transactional
return.
So finding people that agree with your worldview, like you should have some sort of earned secret
as a founder and some sort of unique point of view on the market to get that early traction.
And then who are those people in the market that are going to resonate?
So like at my last company, like health care and insurance is broken.
And we think it sucks for these reasons.
And certain people are going to hear that message and be like, I've been saying this
for years.
I can't believe the insurance companies do this, this and this.
Be like, boom, this person is not going to spreadsheet us and make us like prove the
value in all these different ways and ask for seven different customer testimonials
from a bunch of customers that you don't have yet.
So spending your time on change agents is really, really critical in the early days.
And being honest with them.
Those people aren't necessarily buying your product because they believe it's the best
thing for all of these reasons.
You're a startup.
There's going to be bugs.
There's going to be gaps and there's going to be things that aren't quite where they
need to be.
But they have to believe in the vision and you've got to be transparent with them.
It's like, hey, this is what we are now.
This is what we're building.
These are the things we want to change in the industry and we'd love for you to be a
part of it.
That's a great way to win those early customers.
And then you can translate that to a customer advisory board and you want to obviously have
them be a part of the product creation process if you can.
Let their voice be heard.
Those people will then be your evangelists and do way more than you can with SEO or a
great social presence.
Customers are the thing that matters.
And the other thing I would say in the really early days is just stay involved as a founder
and a founding team.
Because I spent a lot of time with startups and I hear this from a lot of technical founders.
It's like, when should I hire the VP of sales?
When can I get the VP of sales?
When can I have them do the thing?
Because sales is not a comfortable thing to do, especially if you don't come from that
background naturally.
It's not a natural thing.
Oftentimes, technical founders want to get out of sales as quickly as they can and hire
that VP of sales to go figure it out for them.
But stay involved.
People saying no to you in the sales process is the best way to learn what you can invest
in to win deals.
No one's going to believe anybody in your company more than the founder.
The credibility of a VP of sales versus a CEO or the CTO or the COO is totally different.
I encourage founders to get involved heavily in sales early.
Stay involved for longer than they would probably like.
Get out of the transactional stuff.
You don't need to come to first meetings.
You don't need to be sending emails, which you might do in the bootstrap days.
Come to the big meetings with the big customers.
Come to hit the roadshow with your sales team sometimes.
I think that goes a long way.
You mentioned something.
You said that sales is an inorganic process, but wouldn't you say that every single day
that we wake up, we're selling ourselves, right?
Whether it's that new career transition that we want to do or it's that next girlfriend
or boyfriend that we want to meet or talk to, that kind of aligns with a little bit
of sales mythology in terms of opening and closing to some degree, right?
So can you maybe expand a little bit on maybe your contrarian viewpoint to how sales is
a little bit more inorganic for people?
So I do agree with your point, and Daniel Pink has a great book called To Sell as Human
that talks about this, and it's a bit of a reframing.
Everything we do is sales, so get comfortable doing sales as a craft.
It's not that I disagree, but I just think it's still uncomfortable.
Asking people for money, having a lot of people tell you no, especially in the early days,
that's not something we're super well built for without training.
It's like anything else.
You got to practice it and you got to get a bunch of reps to get good at it, especially
as Canadians.
I would say being pretty amicable, it's a generalization, but it's true in a lot of
ways.
We're not New Yorkers.
It's not something that comes really easily to us, so you got to lean in.
You just got to put in the work and be uncomfortable, and there's a lot of great outcomes that come
from that.
For some of the seasoned vets, what should they be looking out for, especially as we
still face uncertainty in the markets ahead?
You provided some really tangible, hands-on feedback for the early-stage startups, but
is there anything that you'd say to some of the more established companies that are still
trying to find inroads or pivots in this market?
First off, I'll frame this as I'm of the opinion that winter is coming.
The economy is being propped up by government stimulus, and at some point, that needs to
run out.
It looks like we're headed to harder economic times.
That's sort of where I'm coming from.
I think when things get really challenging, the fundamentals matter even more.
It's not like a different set of things are all of a sudden important, but we just can't
get away with some of the things that were less than ideal before.
If you read Challenger, the Challenger sales methodology, it's really based on what was
successful in the last downturn.
Those principles still hold true in a good economy.
What makes you a great salesperson?
Do you have an opinion?
Can you share stuff that's insightful to your customer and be seen as more than just a salesperson?
Can you teach the buyer something?
Can you tailor your product to be really closely aligned with what the customer needs?
Can you take control of a sales cycle?
That's the framework from Challenger, and that is still true today.
Can you teach?
Can you tailor?
Can you take control?
I think the basics become even more important, and you're going to see where all the cracks
are in your business as things get tougher.
You're going to see, does your product really add value?
Do people really see a massive benefit from doing business with you, or is this one of
the line items that they're like, yeah, it's pretty good, but we could live without it?
I think asking yourself those tough questions is important to do now versus later because
you got to lean into your customers.
If you think that it's going to be hard to acquire and there's going to be churn risk,
go pay attention to your customers, figure out what you can do to help them, do things
that are maybe not as scalable longer term.
Improve the service that you're giving them and be really transparent with how you're
performing as a company.
It's all about the customer.
It all comes back to, do your customers like doing business with you?
Do they get a lot of value, and are they going to stick with you when things get tough?
I think that's the most important question to ask ourselves because you need to be able
to protect your base.
It's even more important.
We all know the stats.
It's way more expensive to acquire a new customer than it is to hold on to existing revenue.
That becomes even more critical.
Then the other question I would ask is, where are we spending money now that we probably
won't be spending money if all of a sudden we need to cut our budget by 25% or 50% and
extend our runway and do all the things that startups need to be able to do?
Answers will come up pretty fast.
Is there a target market that is more aspirational?
Are we trying to do SMB and enterprise at the same time and splitting our focus and
getting minimal returns from one of them?
Are we trying to get up and running in a new market before we're really ready for that?
You know when that time comes.
The UK is getting scrapped or your South American expansion is going to get tabled.
Think about doing some of those things earlier rather than later because it's probably a
distraction anyways.
Love it.
So if we switch gears a little bit and I mean we've been talking a lot about sales mythology
and I think if we zoom out a little bit to focus more on leadership just in general especially
as it relates both to your career at Shopify and your personal involvement in the greater
tech industry.
Would you say that there are leadership principles you've discovered and executed that have led
to your success?
And you know what do you what did you do to ensure that you continue to grow and develop
as a leader?
Yeah.
So a couple of things that I think are really important to my to my growth to here and just
how I think about building great teams like one is servant leadership.
I would say that's probably the most important principle I have and it answers a lot of questions
like you don't need to go read a hundred leadership books if you truly have a servant
leadership mentality and you really are on a day to day basis thinking about how you
can invest in your team consistently and enthusiastically and helping them advance as people and especially
in sales you see this mentality a lot that like a salesperson is coin operated and they're
only valuable to me in terms of the revenue they generate and like I'm gonna discard them
and hire new ones like there's a quite a transactional relationship that you see in the sales realm
and it's a it's a legacy of a past time and if you read anything about high-performance
teams that's the opposite way to run an organization like what creates engagement retention what
creates high performance you can read a bunch of the Google work about about psychological
safety and a bunch of the employee engagement studies like what creates real engagement
like do you trust your and like your boss do you believe in the mission are you learning
and growing do you see a career path and do you think that and do your values align with
the values of the company like it's it isn't really rocket science but I think where we
go wrong is oftentimes we read a bunch of leadership stuff and we think about them as
tools to then make people do what we want and it's all about the business outcome and
we forget that it's like well what if I thought first from the the employees perspective like
what do they really want and how do I build towards that well at the same time building
towards a business outcome and usually your answer is like help them grow in their career
them good skills treat them nicely like be transparent don't like try to tell them one
thing when you know something else is going on like that consistently will come back to bite
you and a lot of that seems obvious like just treat people well be in and prioritize them just
as much as you prioritize the business outcome because like I'm not gonna get into all the
reasons but like that's the path like you'll hold on to your best people people will give
you great outcomes when things aren't going well you'll hear about them really quickly
